assertion_analysis.assertions: a reservation keyed on attempt 3 beside a worker record naming attempt 2 is still held, and a second reserve raises CrewError
assertion_analysis.fails_if: the guard call at reckon/crew/recovery_liveness.py:1168 is removed: the run then reads as parked, held_launch_reservation returns None through dispatch_launch.py:2602, and both assertions redden. The comparison is against the production read, not against a value the test supplied, so it is independent of its input.

assertion_analysis.assertions: the station's own refresh stage really entered the monkeypatched publish, so the tick is blocking
assertion_analysis.fails_if: run_station stops routing its per-project refresh through station_obligations.publish, or stops being driven; it is a harness-fidelity assertion rather than a guard on the landed behaviour.

assertion_analysis.assertions: the tick had not returned at the moment of the wake
assertion_analysis.fails_if: ticker.is_alive() is False, that is run_station returned before the wake. The gate.is_set() operand cannot fail, because gate is set only in the finally at line 375.

assertion_analysis.assertions: the sweep offered a resume while the tick was held
assertion_analysis.fails_if: no resume is recorded within the 30-second wall-clock drain; at the base revision this is the line that fails, as test-logs/negative-control.log records.

assertion_analysis.assertions: the wake arrived within 300 seconds of the run's injected clock after the probe turned terminal
assertion_analysis.fails_if: the code under test needs more than thirty clock reads between the terminal write and the resume, which a tick-paced wake would. Both sides read the same counter, but their distance is set by how often the station's own threads call clock(), so the assertion tracks the code, though it measures latency in reads rather than in asserted run-clock minutes.

assertion_analysis.assertions: no station sweep raised during the case
assertion_analysis.fails_if: resumption.sweep raises for any reason, which the wrapper records before re-raising.

findings.summary: `_latest_reservation` and `_attempt_number` re-implement the reservation-file enumeration, name parse and safe read that reckon/crew/dispatch_launch.py already owns.
findings.text: non-blocking: the new pair globs `attempt-*.reservation`, pulls the attempt out of the file name with a manual split, and reads each payload with its own json.loads plus Mapping check. dispatch_launch owns those three steps for the same file family, at `_reservation_taken_by_this_process` (dispatch_launch.py:2376), `_RESERVATION_PATTERN` (:2262) and `_read_reservation` (:2416), and recovery_liveness already imports dispatch_launch lazily in the other direction (recovery_liveness.py:659), so the owner was reachable. The addition duplicates rather than extends the owner, so two name parsers now have to agree on what an `attempt-N.reservation` file is.

findings.summary: `_seconds_from_stamp` re-implements `reckon._timestamps.parse_utc`, which this module already imports at recovery_liveness.py:12 and uses at :506.
findings.text: non-blocking: the new helper parses an ISO timestamp with `datetime.fromisoformat` and returns epoch seconds, which is what `parse_utc` does for this module (reckon/_timestamps.py:36), including a Z suffix, a numeric offset and a bare ISO string. The module imports it at line 12 and calls it at :506, so the owner is in hand and this forks it; the two also disagree on breadth, since parse_utc accepts a numeric epoch and `_seconds_from_stamp` refuses every non-string.

findings.summary: The `gate.is_set() is False` operand is inert, because nothing sets `gate` before the finally block, so it cannot fail and cannot detect a tick that already returned.
findings.text: non-blocking: `gate` is set only by the case's own finally at line 375, so at line 353 that operand is False whatever the station does, and the claim that the tick was still held when the wake happened rests on `ticker.is_alive()` alone. The shape was recorded for `held_tick` at line 272 in the earlier review of this file and is now half-repaired: `gate` is genuinely read by the monkeypatched `station_obligations.publish`, so the tick really does block, but the operand that names the hold is still vacuous and would pass a tick that `gate.wait(timeout=60)` had already released.

findings.summary: The half-hour length of the tick hold is asserted nowhere in run-clock terms, although the manifest and the fragment both state it; the injected clock advances only when read, so CLOCK_STEP_SECONDS alone fixes no span.
findings.text: non-blocking: `clock()` and `now_of_run_clock()` both advance one itertools.count, so a virtual second passes only when some thread reads the clock, and the total virtual span of the hold is a function of how often the station happens to read it. The case does prove the fact that matters, that the tick had not returned while the wake happened, but the manifest's 'the station's clock is injected so the case can hold the tick for thirty minutes of the run's own time' and the fragment's 'half an hour of the run's own time' are claims no assertion in the case measures.
